items.title: Assess each security header against an actual browser exposure
items.objective: Determine whether a missing, malformed, or weak header creates a reachable security consequence for the response type and threat model.
prerequisites: Representative responses, routes, status codes, browser contexts, and target browser support
A confirmed underlying exposure or threat model before rating a missing header as a vulnerability
steps: Inventory the header and effective policy on representative success, redirect, error, authenticated, download, and cached responses
Parse duplicate/malformed values and identify which browser/proxy policy actually applies
Exercise only a harmless controlled browser behavior relevant to the response and threat model
Confirm meaningful security impact and exclude checklist-only or obsolete-header findings

examples.note: A missing header is not a vulnerability by itself; demonstrate relevant browser behavior and realistic impact.

items.manipulate: The response route/status/browser context and one policy directive or header value at a time
items.secure_behavior: The response sends a valid, context-appropriate, consistently enforced browser policy that addresses a real exposure without relying on obsolete controls.
items.vulnerable_behavior: a relevant browser behavior remains exploitable and the header would materially prevent or reduce it
items.validation: Demonstrate effective behavior in a supported browser and the underlying exposure; scanner output, absence, or syntax differences alone are insufficient.
false_positives: a scanner checklist can flag headers irrelevant to an API/download/static resource
application controls can remove the underlying exposure independently
items.impact: Impact depends on the underlying browser exposure and can include downgrade, script execution amplification, UI redressing, data/referrer leakage, cross-origin resource abuse, stale sensitive data, or unsafe content rendering.
evidence: Raw representative response headers
Parsed effective policy and target browser/version
Harmless controlled browser behavior
Underlying exposure, realistic impact, route consistency, and false-positive exclusions
items.remediation: Configure valid policies from the response threat model, apply them consistently at the trusted edge/application, test supported browsers, fix the underlying weakness, and remove obsolete/conflicting headers.
do_not_report: Do not report header absences as a vulnerability category; report only a demonstrated, reproducible browser exposure that a missing or malformed policy actually enables. Header inventories belong in the assessment appendix, not the findings section.

A confirmed underlying exposure or threat model before rating a missing header as a vulnerability
steps: Inventory the header and effective policy on representative success, redirect, error, authenticated, download, and cached responses
Parse duplicate/malformed values and identify which browser/proxy policy actually applies
Exercise only a harmless controlled browser behavior relevant to the response and threat model
Confirm meaningful security impact and exclude checklist-only or obsolete-header findings

examples.note: A missing header is not a vulnerability by itself; demonstrate relevant browser behavior and realistic impact.

items.manipulate: The response route/status/browser context and one policy directive or header value at a time
items.secure_behavior: The response sends a valid, context-appropriate, consistently enforced browser policy that addresses a real exposure without relying on obsolete controls.
items.vulnerable_behavior: documented full-client cleanup fails and leaves reusable synthetic authority/data
items.validation: Demonstrate effective behavior in a supported browser and the underlying exposure; scanner output, absence, or syntax differences alone are insufficient.
false_positives: ordinary logout can invalidate server sessions without clearing every preference/cache
Clear-Site-Data support and scope vary by browser
items.impact: Impact depends on the underlying browser exposure and can include downgrade, script execution amplification, UI redressing, data/referrer leakage, cross-origin resource abuse, stale sensitive data, or unsafe content rendering.
evidence: Raw representative response headers
Parsed effective policy and target browser/version
Harmless controlled browser behavior
Underlying exposure, realistic impact, route consistency, and false-positive exclusions
items.remediation: Configure valid policies from the response threat model, apply them consistently at the trusted edge/application, test supported browsers, fix the underlying weakness, and remove obsolete/conflicting headers.
do_not_report: Do not report absent Clear-Site-Data as a finding; it is an optional hygiene control. Report only when logout or reset leaves observable sensitive state behind and standard cache and storage controls fail to clear it.
